doc.title: Burrill Crohn interviewed by Monk Rowe, Woodstock, New York, January 3, 2012

chapter: Hearing jazz and learning the camera
title: Hearing jazz live in New York clubs
summary: Growing up in New York, he heard swing, 52nd Street, Roy Eldridge, Bird, Mingus, Monk, Coltrane and Miles, not always knowing they were legendary.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: How about your experience hearing jazz live in clubs? Did it happen early on for you?
Yes. I mean as soon as I was old enough to get into a club, and even when I couldn’t. Yeah I was lucky. I grew up in New York. I was born in Paris but I moved when I was

very young, and there was jazz everywhere in New York back then. And my early taste was to swing, because the people I listened to were the big bands and Harry James. I remember finding an early recording of Harry James where he played a great recording. He played in a small group in Chicago. It was unbelievable, that small group stuff. And I remember going to 52nd Street and hearing Wilbur and Sidney DeParis. You know who they are. And then, but then I heard Roy Eldridge and I actually heard Bird before he died, just once in a little club, what was it called, I can’t remember. I know it was on the corner of Third and MacDougal — The Open Door. That’s what it’s called. And as I grew older I heard a lot of people. I heard Mingus and Monk. I heard Coltrane.
Can you recall, at the time, however old you were, were you aware that you were listening to legendary people?

Excellent question, excellent question. No I don’t think so, looking back. By the time I first heard Miles I knew he was legendary. I heard Miles at Café Bohemia. But by and large — and the other thing was you could go out and hear the legends but you could also go hear someone you never heard of play just as good and by whatever chance of fate or their own personality they never made it quote, the way the others did. I’ve talked to musicians who have stories who have traveled all over the country — they’ll go to a little club somewhere in a nowhere town and they hear a musician as great as anybody you’d ever hear. So there are a lot of geniuses out there that never saw the light of day. So I’m not sure how I felt. Because I grew up at a point where some of the people I heard were already becoming legendary like Monk and Mingus, so I was a little swayed by that. At the same time they were still young men. It’s sort of like a little bit of each.
